findings.evidence: Honey bees collect floral nectar, which varies by plant and generally contains far more water than ripe honey.
Invertase breaks sucrose into glucose and fructose; glucose oxidase also contributes to honey's transformation chemistry.
Workers deposit nectar into wax cells and fan air through the hive; evaporation substantially concentrates the sugars.
Mature honey has low available water and is often sealed with a wax cap; moisture thresholds vary across definitions and standards.
Commercial extraction and later handling are beekeeper steps after bees have stored and capped ripe honey.

editorial_angles: Show the colony as a coordinated processing system, not a lone bee performing every step.
Explain the difference between the bee's honey stomach (transport crop) and its digestive stomach.
Separate enzymatic sugar changes from physical evaporation; both matter.
Treat moisture percentages as ranges affected by nectar and conditions, not one magic number.
Distinguish natural ripening from beekeeper extraction and later food processing.
